The Quiet Return of Night Trains

By Ada Fielding

Share

When the last sleeper service between Paris and Berlin was cancelled in 2014, few expected to see it again. A decade later, the route is back, and its cabins sell out weeks in advance.

Operators say demand grew 3.5 times faster than they forecast. "We underestimated how many people want to arrive rested," said one planner, who asked not to be named.

SLEEPER TRAIN PRICES ARE RISING FASTER THAN FLIGHTS, NEW DATA SHOWS

Passengers board the overnight service in Vienna. (Example Rail)

Why travellers are switching

Cost is part of it. A bed on a night train replaces both a flight and a hotel, and the journey begins and ends in city centres rather than distant airports.

Advertisement

  • No security queues or baggage fees.
  • A full night's sleep while travelling.
  • Lower emissions than flying the same distance.

The train is the hotel. That is the whole idea.

Still, the business is fragile. Rolling stock is expensive, track access fees vary by country, and a single late connection can ripple across an entire timetable.

For now, though, the trains are full. "Every new route we open sells," the planner said. "That has not happened in my career before."
